blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Explain why earnings differ between occupations, read the pattern in earnings figures, and describe in words the market forces behind a difference in pay.

blocks.heading: The reasons behind a pay gap
blocks.text: Earnings - the pay a worker receives over a period, including overtime and bonuses - differ because occupations differ. Skill and qualifications: a chartered accountant's work demands years of study. Scarcity: where few people hold what employers need, pay rises. Experience and responsibility: a mine shift supervisor answers for others and earns more than a new hire. Risk and conditions: a long-haul driver earns more than a pump attendant with a similar training period, because the job takes the driver from home for days at a stretch and employers must pay enough to keep people in it. Productivity and the balance of demand and supply in the occupation set the rest, and where a small number of large employers fix pay scales, their scales hold earnings down.

blocks.heading: Reading the gaps
blocks.text: A 2026 survey of average monthly earnings in Namibia found a petrol-station attendant on N$4 800, a school teacher with ten years in the job on N$14 200, and a chartered accountant on N$38 000. The accountant earns N$38 000 - N$4 800 = N$33 200 more than the attendant. Qualifying takes years of study and fees, few complete it, and employers compete for those who do. The teacher also holds a degree, yet many qualified teachers apply for posts against pay scales set by a small number of large employers, so the scarcity premium is missing. In Brazil, certified welders in the Rio Grande shipyards earn well above general welders for the same reason: certification is scarce, and the yards bid for it.

blocks.heading: The forces behind a difference, drawn in words
blocks.text: Picture the market for certified water engineers. The vertical axis measures the monthly wage in N$; the horizontal axis measures the number of certified engineers. At a low wage few engineers offer their services and employers seek many, so the number sought exceeds the number offered; at a high wage the reverse holds. The two lines cross at the wage where the numbers match. When new water-treatment projects raise the demand for engineers, the demand line moves outward: at the old wage employers now seek more engineers than the region holds, so the wage is bid up until the numbers match again at a higher wage, with more engineers at work. Over the years that follow, the higher wage draws students into training, the supply line moves outward too, and the premium narrows - provided employers' demand has stopped growing faster than the new supply.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The scarcity that lifts some earnings begins in the training choices of this topic; the demand behind a rising wage traces back to product demand in topic 2.3; the employers doing the bidding are the firms of topic 3.5; and persistent pay gaps are one focus of the government's role in topic 4.1.
